uncited: It builds on [Neighbor Counting](2905-neighbor-counting.md) by using range-queries to evaluate local point density.
**Inputs:** A dataset $P$ of points, a search radius $\varepsilon$ (eps), and a minimum number of points $minPts$.
**Outputs:** A label for each point in $P$: a cluster ID (integer $\ge 0$), or NOISE.
- **Core-point:** A point $p$ is a core-point if the number of points in its $\varepsilon$-neighborhood $V_\varepsilon(p)$ is $\ge minPts$.
- **Border-point:** A point $p_a$ is a border-point if it is density-reachable from a core-point $p_b$ but $|V_\varepsilon(p_a)| < minPts$.
For each point $p \in P$, set $labels[p] \leftarrow \text{UNCLASSIFIED}$.
If $labels[p] \neq \text{UNCLASSIFIED}$, continue.
Call $ExpandCluster(p, \varepsilon, minPts, P, labels, clusterID)$.
If $ExpandCluster$ returns `True` (meaning $p$ was a core-point and a cluster was formed), increment $clusterID \leftarrow clusterID + 1$.
Perform a range-query on $P$ with center $p$ and radius $\varepsilon$ to retrieve all neighbors $N_p$.
Initialize $S$ as a list containing all points in $N_p$ except $p$.
If it was previously labeled NOISE from a prior failed expansion, it should be updated to the current cluster if it is now reachable.
The source implies border points are reachable from core points.
If $q$ was NOISE, it is now a border point of the current cluster).
If $labels[q] \neq \text{UNCLASSIFIED}$, continue.
Perform a range-query on $P$ with center $q$ and radius $\varepsilon$ to retrieve neighbors $N_q$.
If $labels[r] == \text{UNCLASSIFIED}$, add $r$ to $S$.
Typical values depend on the scale of the data.
Typical values are $\ge 4$ for low-dimensional data.
- If $minPts$ is too high, most points may be labeled NOISE.
- If $\varepsilon$ is too small, clusters may be fragmented.
- Precision issues in distance calculations near the boundary $\varepsilon$ can affect core-point classification.
HDBSCAN is a hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm.
It constructs a cluster hierarchy using a minimum spanning tree of the mutual reachability graph.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ to store the dataset and labels.
- **When to use:** When clusters are non-convex and of varying densities, and noise is present.
- **When not to use:** When clusters are convex and of similar density (K-Means is better), or when data dimensionality is very high (curse of distance).
It is widely used in spatial data mining, volume exploration, and clustering of point clouds.
